strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated limitation of prior GRF methods (Choromanski 2023; Reid et al. 2023/2024): the inherently sequential nature of long random walks limits both computational efficiency and expressiveness for distant node pairs. The walk-stitching idea (concatenating shorter, parallelizable walks while preserving unbiasedness) is a clean and non-trivial technical contribution.

Solid theoretical backing: the paper proves unbiasedness of the stitching mechanism under a general termination scheme (Lemma 3.1, generalizing Lemma 2.1), derives a closed-form MSE expression for degree l=2 (Lemma 3.2), and proves a monotonic-improvement result for degrees that are powers of two (Theorem 3.3). Proofs are included in the appendix and appear rigorous.

The generalized termination strategy (replacing the fixed Bernoulli halting scheme with arbitrary discrete distributions, e.g., Poisson) is a nice, low-cost extension that is shown empirically to improve accuracy at no extra parallel-compute cost.

Broad and diverse empirical evaluation: kernel approximation error across 8 graphs of varying size/topology, accuracy specifically on long-diameter graphs (Peptides, CIFAR, Reddit-Binary, GeometricShapes, etc.), and three downstream tasks (graph classification, node clustering, mesh vertex-normal prediction) with consistent gains over regular GRFs and near-parity with the exact (brute-force) kernel.

Useful ablation isolating the specific contribution of walk-stitching by re-using the exact same underlying random walks as the GRF baseline, which cleanly disentangles the stitching mechanism's benefit from sampling more walks.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility/appendix material: hyperparameter choices, dataset statistics, and mesh IDs are all specified, aiding replication even though code is not yet released.
weaknesses: The wall-clock speed comparison (Fig. 5, 'Computational Time') is not fully convincing: it reports 'Walk Time' and 'Stitching Time' separately decreasing with degree, but does not clearly present total end-to-end runtime versus baseline GRFs on real parallel hardware, nor discuss how well the claimed GPU parallelism is actually realized in practice (e.g., wall-clock latency under batched GPU execution vs. CPU sequential simulation).

Theorem 3.3 (monotonic MSE improvement) is only proven for degrees that are powers of two, leaving open whether monotonic improvement holds for general stitching degree l, which is a gap between the theoretical claim and the practically used range of degrees (2-6) shown in the experiments.

The overhead of the general termination strategy (computing tail probabilities τ(k)=P(X≥k) for arbitrary distributions, needed in the modified update rule) is not analyzed; this could offset some of the claimed 'no extra computational cost' benefit for distributions where τ(k) is not cheap to compute.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to the existing GRF literature (Choromanski 2023; Reid et al. 2023, 2024a, 2024b): the core idea is essentially a convolution/factorization trick for combining GRF outputs, and the significance is fairly specialized to the graph-kernel-approximation community rather than broader ML.

Presentation is dense in places, particularly the matrix bookkeeping for Option I/II/III (Eqs. 5-7) and the notation-heavy proofs, which may hinder accessibility; some notation (e.g., mixing p and t as walk-length variables, overloaded X/Y symbols) could be streamlined.
Code is not released with the submission (promised only upon acceptance), which somewhat limits immediate reproducibility despite the otherwise detailed methodological description.

No comparison against alternative long-range kernel approximation strategies outside the GRF family (e.g., sparse iterative solvers, other random-feature or low-rank approximation techniques), making it hard to judge how GRFs++ stacks up against the broader landscape of scalable graph kernel computation methods.

strengths: The paper introduces two well-motivated extensions to Graph Random Features (GRFs): a walk-stitching mechanism that composes short random walks (amenable to parallel/matrix computation) to emulate long walks, and a generalized walk-termination scheme beyond the Bernoulli halting rule. Both are non-trivial generalizations addressing genuine, previously identified weaknesses of GRFs (sequential sampling cost, poor modeling of distant-node relationships).

Solid theoretical grounding: unbiasedness is proven in a fairly general setting (Lemma 2.1/3.1, connecting the construction to higher-order de-convolutions of the kernel's generating function), a closed-form MSE expression is derived for degree l=2 (Lemma 3.2), and a monotonic improvement result with stitching degree is shown (Theorem 3.3), with detailed proofs in the appendix.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: kernel approximation accuracy across 8+ synthetic/real graphs, targeted analysis of long-distance node pairs on large-diameter graphs, ablations isolating the walk-stitching effect from walk reuse, wall-clock speed comparisons against brute-force kernel construction on large meshes, and four diverse downstream tasks (ViT attention masking, graph classification, node clustering, mesh normal prediction) plus integration into GraphGPS/Performer. Results are consistently favorable for GRFs++ relative to regular GRFs.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: hyperparameters, dataset statistics, and experimental protocols are documented in the appendix, and the authors state they will open-source code.
weaknesses: Theorem 3.3 (accuracy improves monotonically with stitching degree) is only proven for degrees that are powers of two, yet the abstract/intro imply a general benefit of increasing stitching degree; the gap between the general claim and the restricted proof is not clearly flagged in the main text.

The paper empirically recommends reusing the same set of random walks across the l components of GRFs++ (breaking the independence assumption required for unbiasedness), reporting this 'performs well in practice,' but provides no theoretical characterization of the resulting bias or its magnitude — this is an important practical deviation from the proven guarantees that is under-analyzed.

Several experimental choices (e.g., fixing stitching degree l=2 for most downstream tasks, hyperparameter sweeps for baselines vs. proposed method) are not deeply justified, and it is unclear how sensitive results are to these choices or how they were selected (risk of some selection favoring the proposed method).

In the graph classification comparisons, the paper acknowledges its kernel is an intra-graph (node) kernel while most baselines are inter-graph kernels, making the 'competitive performance' claims only loosely comparable; the practical significance of this comparison is therefore limited.

Presentation is dense in places, with some inconsistent notation across sections (e.g., ξρ(i) in Algorithm 1 vs. φf(i)/ϕf(i) in the text, and K1^(i) vs. K_1^i indexing), which could hinder reproducibility for a reader trying to precisely align the algorithm boxes with the theoretical statements.
The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with any potential limitations or societal implications specific to this work.
